entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.1-Deut.4.8">Deu 4:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen2178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2179" type="x-p"/> The Israelites were to hearken to the laws and rights which Moses taught to do (that they were to do), that they might live and attain to the possession of the land which the Lord would give them. “Hearkening” involves laying to heart and observing. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.9">Deu 4:9</reference> <div eID="gen2184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2185" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Only beware and take care of thyself</hi>.” To “keep the soul,” i.e., to take care of the soul as the seat of life, to defend one’s life from danger and injury (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.3">Pro 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.16">Pro 19:16</reference>). “<hi type="italic">That thou do not forget</hi> את־הדּברים (the facts described in <reference osisRef="Exod.19.24">Ex 19-24</reference>), <), <hi type="italic">and that they do not depart from thy heart all the days of thy life</hi>,” i.e., are not forgotten as long as thou livest, “<hi type="italic">and thou makest them known to thy children and thy children’s children</hi>.” These acts of God formed the foundation of the true religion, the real basis of the covenant legislation, and the firm guarantee of the objective truth and divinity of all the laws and ordinances which Moses gave to the people. And it was this which constituted the essential distinction between the religion of the Old Testament and all heathen religions, whose founders, it is true, professed to derive their doctrines and statutes from divine inspiration, but without giving any practical guarantee that their origin was truly divine.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.10-Deut.4.12">Deu 4:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen2185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2186" type="x-p"/> In the words, “<hi type="italic">The day</hi> (היּום, adverbial accusative) “<hi type="italic">that thou stoodest before Jehovah thy God at Horeb</hi>,” etc., Moses reminds the people of the leading features of those grand events: first of all of the fact that God directed him to gather the people together, that He might make known His words to them (Exo 19:9.), that they were to learn to fear Him all their life long, and to teach their children also (יראה, inf., like שׂנאה, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.27">Deu 1:27</reference>); and secondly (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.11">Deu 4:11</reference>), that they came near to the mountain which burned in fire (cf. Exo 19:17.). The expression, burning in fire “<hi type="italic">even to the heart of heaven</hi>,” i.e., quite into the sky, is a rhetorical description of the awful majesty of the pillar of fire, in which the glory of the Lord appeared upon Sinai, intended to impress deeply upon the minds of the people the remembrance of this manifestation of God. And the expression, “<hi type="italic">darkness, clouds, and thick darkness,</hi>” which is equivalent to the smoking of the great mountain (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference>), is employed with the same object. And lastly (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.12">Deu 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.13">Deu 4:13</reference>), he reminds them that the Lord spoke out of the midst of the fire, and adds this important remark, to prepare the way for what is to follow, “<hi type="italic">Ye heard the sound of the words, but ye did not see a shape,</hi>” which not only agrees most fully with Ex 24, where it is stated that the sight of the glory of Jehovah upon the mountain appeared to the people as they stood at the foot of the mountain “like devouring fire” (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.17">Deu 4:17</reference>), and that even the elders who “saw God” upon the mountain at the conclusion of the covenant saw no form of God (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.11">Deu 4:11</reference>), but also with <reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Exo 33:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.23">Exo 33:23</reference>, according to which no man can see the face (פּנים) of God. Even the similitude (<hi type="italic">Temunah</hi>) of Jehovah, which Moses saw when the Lord spoke to him mouth to mouth (Num 12:8), was not the form of the essential being of God which was visible to his bodily eyes, but simply a manifestation of the glory of God answering to his own intuition and perceptive faculty, which is not to be regarded as a form of God which was an adequate representation of the divine nature. The true God has no such form which is visible to the human eye.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deu 4:19</reference> <div eID="gen2190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2191" type="x-p"/> They were not to allow themselves to be torn away (נדּח) to worship the stars of heaven, namely, by the seductive influence exerted upon the senses by the sight of the heavenly bodies as they shone in their glorious splendour. The reason for this prohibition is given in the relative clause, “<hi type="italic">which Jehovah thy God hath allotted to all nations under the whole heaven</hi>.” The thought is not, “God has given the heathen the sun, moon, and stars for service, i.e., to serve them with their light,” as <hi type="italic">Onkelos, the Rabbins, Jerome,</hi> and others, suppose, but He has allotted them to them for worship, i.e., permitted them to choose them as the objects of their worship, which is the view adopted by <hi type="italic">Justin Martyr, Clemens Alex.,</hi> and others. According to the scriptural view, even the idolatry of the heathen existed by divine permission and arrangement. God gave up the heathen to idolatry and shameful lusts, because, although they knew Him from His works, they did not praise Him as God (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Rom 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Rom 1:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.26">Rom 1:26</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.21-Deut.4.24">Deu 4:21-24</reference> <div eID="gen2192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2193" type="x-p"/> The bringing of Israel out of Egypt reminds Moses of the end, viz., Canaan, and leads him to mention again how the Lord had refused him permission to enter into this good land; and to this he adds the renewed warning not to forget the covenant or make any image of God, since Jehovah, as a jealous God, would never tolerate this. The swearing attributed to God in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.21">Deu 4:21</reference> is neither mentioned in Num 20 nor at the announcement of Moses’ death in Num 27:12.; but it is not to be called in question on that account, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.25-Deut.4.26">Deu 4:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen2194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2195" type="x-p"/> If the Israelites should beget children and children’s children, and grow old in the land, and then should make images of God, and do that which was displeasing to God to provoke Him; in that case Moses called upon heaven and earth as witnesses against them, that they should be quickly destroyed out of the land. “<hi type="italic">Growing old in the land</hi>” involved forgetfulness of the former manifestations of grace on the part of the Lord, but not necessarily becoming voluptuous through the enjoyment of the riches of the land, although this might also lead to forgetfulness of God and the manifestations of His grace (cf. Deu 6:10., <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>). The apodosis commences with Deu 4:26. העיד, with בּ and the accusative, to take or summon as a witness against a person. Heaven and earth do not stand here for the rational beings dwelling in them, but are personified, represented as living, and capable of sensation and speech, and mentioned as witnesses who would raise up against Israel, not to proclaim its guilt, but to bear witness that God, the Lord of heaven and earth, had warned the people, and, as it is described in the parallel passage in <reference osisRef="Deut.30.19">Deu 30:19</reference>, had set before them the choice of life and death, and therefore was just in punishing them for their unfaithfulness (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.6">Psa 50:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Psa 51:6</reference>). “Prolong days,” as in Exo 20:12.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.27">Deu 4:27</reference> <div eID="gen2195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2196" type="x-p"/> Jehovah would scatter them among the nations, where they would perish through want and suffering, and only a few (מספּר מתי, <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference>) would be left. “Whither” refers to the nations whose land is thought of (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.12.29">Deu 12:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.3">Deu 30:3</reference>). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">Deu 4:28</reference> <div eID="gen2196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2197" type="x-p"/> There among the heathen they would be obliged to serve gods that were the work of men’s hands, gods of wood and stone, that could neither hear, nor eat, nor smell, i.e., possessed no senses, showed no sign of life. What Moses threatens here, follows from the eternal laws of the divine government. The more refined idolatry of image-worship leads to coarser and coarser forms, in which the whole nature of idol-worship is manifested in all its pitiableness. “When once the God of revelation is forsaken, the God of reason and imagination must also soon be given up and make way for still lower powers, that perfectly accord with the I exalted upon the throne, and in the time of pretended 'illumination' to atheism and materialism also” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.32-Deut.4.34">Deu 4:32-34</reference> <div eID="gen2199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2200" type="x-p"/> But in order to accomplish something more than merely preserving the people from apostasy by the threat of punishment, namely, to secure a more faithful attachment and continued obedience to His commands by awakening the feeling of cordial love, Moses reminds them again of the glorious miracles of divine grace performed in connection with the election and deliverance of Israel, such as had never been heard of from the beginning of the world; and with this strong practical proof of the love of the true God, he brings his first address to a close. This closing thought in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.32">Deu 4:32</reference> is connected by כּי (<hi type="italic">for</hi>) with the leading idea in Deu 4:31. “Jehovah thy God is a merciful God,” to show that the sole ground for the election and redemption of Israel was the compassion of God towards the human race. “<hi type="italic">For ask now of the days that are past, from the day that God created man upon the earth, and from one end of the heaven unto the other, whether so great a thing has ever happened, or anything of the kind has been heard of:</hi>” i.e., the history of all times since the creation of man, and of all places under the whole heaven, can relate no such events as those which have happened to Israel, viz., at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.33">Deu 4:33</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.12">Deu 4:12</reference>). From this awfully glorious manifestation of God, Moses goes back in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference> to the miracles with which God effected the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt. “<hi type="italic">Or has a god attempted</hi> (made the attempt) <hi type="italic">to come and take to himself people from people</hi> (i.e., to fetch the people of Israel out of the midst of the Egyptian nation), <hi type="italic">with temptations</hi> (the events in Egypt by which Pharaoh’s relation to the Lord was put to the test; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.6.22">Deu 6:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.7.18-Deut.7.19">Deu 7:18-19</reference>), with signs and wonders (the Egyptian plagues, see <reference osisRef="Exod.7.3">Exo 7:3</reference>), <hi type="italic">and with conflict</hi> (at the Red Sea: <reference osisRef="Exod.14.14">Exo 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.3">Exo 15:3</reference>), <hi type="italic">and with a strong hand and outstretched arm</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Exod.6.6">Exo 6:6</reference>), <hi type="italic">and with great terrors?</hi>” In the three points mentioned last, all the acts of God in Egypt are comprehended, according to both cause and effect. They were revelations of the omnipotence of the Lord, and produced great terrors (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.12.30-Exod.12.36">Exo 12:30-36</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.37-Deut.4.38">Deu 4:37-38</reference> <div eID="gen2202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2203" type="x-p"/> All this He did from love to the fathers of Israel (the patriarchs): “<hi type="italic">and indeed because He loved thy fathers, He chose his seed </hi>(the seed of Abraham, the first of the patriarchs) <hi type="italic">after him, and brought thee</hi> (Israel) <hi type="italic">out of Egypt by His face with great power, to drive out...and to bring thee, to give thee their land...so that thou mightest know and take to heart...and keep His laws</hi>,” etc. With regard to the construction of these verses, the clause כּי ותחת (and because) in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.37">Deu 4:37</reference> is not to be regarded as dependent upon what precedes, as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> supposes; nor are <reference osisRef="Deut.4.37">Deu 4:37</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.4.38">Deu 4:38</reference> to be taken as the protasis, and <reference osisRef="Deut.4.39">Deu 4:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.40">Deu 4:40</reference> as the apodosis (as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> maintains). Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> pp. 265, 266). - <hi type="italic">Golan</hi>, in <hi type="italic">Bashan</hi>, according to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v. Gaulon</hi> or <hi type="italic">Golan</hi>), was still a very large village in Batanaea even in his day, from which the district generally received the name of <hi type="italic">Gaulonitis</hi> or <hi type="italic">Joan</hi>; but it has not yet been discovered again.
